    Meta cells with bixverse¶

    Python port of the R vignette Meta cells with bixverse. Original author: Gregor Lueg.

    Intro¶

    Meta cells are small groups of transcriptionally similar cells aggregated into a single representative profile. The motivation is twofold: firstly, single cell counts are sparse and noisy, and many downstream methods (correlation networks, GRN inference, archetype-based modelling) behave poorly on raw single cell data. Aggregating into meta cells reduces sparsity while preserving the heterogeneity that bulk pseudo-replicates would average out. Secondly, they reduce the computational burden substantially.

    bixverse provides four meta cell algorithms with different underlying ideas:

    • hdWGCNA-style meta cells (Morabito, et al., 2023) iterate over a kNN graph, picking seed cells and aggregating their neighbours, with a constraint on how many cells two meta cells are allowed to share. Simple, fast and reasonably effective. Works directly on a kNN graph.
    • SEACells (Persad, et al., 2023) uses kernel archetypal analysis. The algorithm finds a set of archetypes (the SEACells) such that every cell can be expressed as a convex combination of nearby archetypes. Tends to produce purer aggregations but is the most computationally expensive of the four.
    • SuperCells (Bilous, et al., 2022) applies the walktrap community detection algorithm to the kNN graph and treats each community as a meta cell. Granularity is controlled indirectly through a graining factor (the average number of cells per meta cell).
    • MetaCells2 (Ben-Kiki, et al., 2022) works on the raw counts and builds its own similarity graph, no embedding or kNN needed. It aims for meta cells of a target size and UMI count, splits the cells into piles, and leaves cells it cannot place convincingly unassigned.

    One implementation detail worth flagging upfront. The SingleCells class keeps counts on disk in DuckDB and binary Rust-based files and streams them in as needed. The MetaCells class does not. After aggregation the count matrix is small enough to hold entirely in memory as a sparse matrix, and all downstream operations (HVG, PCA, neighbours, clustering, embeddings) run against this in-memory representation (most of the code still runs in Rust nonetheless). Practically that means the meta cell pipeline is substantially faster than the equivalent operations on the parent SingleCells object for two reasons: data is already in memory and more importantly, it is simply less data.

    Preparing the single cell data¶

    We use the same CD34 cells from the SEACells vignette to set up the parent SingleCells object: load (QC not needed, it's already filtered data), HVG selection, PCA, kNN graph. We can use the provided cell type labels to check purity.

    Generating meta cells¶

    All four generators take a SingleCells object, read counts from the binary files as needed, and return a MetaCells object. They share a common output structure: an obs table with one row per meta cell (recording which original cells went into it), a var table mirrored from the parent object, and an in-memory sparse count matrix.

    hdWGCNA-style (bootstrapped metacells)¶

    The hdWGCNA-style algorithm reuses the kNN graph already on the object. The two parameters that matter most are target_no_metacells and max_shared, which controls how many cells two meta cells may have in common. The original paper uses 1000 meta cells, but we want to also compare the different metrics downstream, so we will set it to 250. We also recalculate the kNN graph with larger k, to include more cells per given meta cell.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    hdwgcna = bv.metacells.generate_bt_meta_cells(
    sc,
    params=BtMetacellsParams(target_no_metacells=250, k=25),
    # regenerate the kNN graph with 25 neighbours
    regenerate_knn=True,
    verbose=True,
)
assert hdwgcna is not None

    Importantly, not all cells HAVE to be assigned to a meta cell and cells can occur in several meta cells at once. A number of cells remains unassigned and each meta cell contains self + neighbours, i.e., 26 (self + k = 25) original cells. How often do the cells occur... ?

    SEACells¶

    SEACells operates on the PCA embedding (or any batch corrected embedding) and the kNN graph and runs an iterative kernel archetypal analysis. n_sea_cells sets the number of archetypes; min_iter/max_iter bound the optimisation; convergence_epsilon sets the early stopping threshold relative to the initial RSS. The algorithm was aggressively optimised to be faster. With pruning=True (default) small values are set to zero, removing basically dust and accelerating the calculations substantially. The rule of thumb by the authors is one SEACell per 75 cells, i.e., 90 SEACells for this experiment. We will set this higher here to 250 to make this a bit more comparable with the other methods...

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    seacells = bv.metacells.generate_seacells(
    sc,
    SeacellsParams(n_sea_cells=250, min_iter=10, convergence_epsilon=0.001),
    verbose=True,
)

    SEACells on large data¶

    SEACells is infamous for being very slow and difficult to run on larger data sets. Most of the hot path has been rewritten in bixverse, which is what makes the algorithm feasible beyond a few tens of thousands of cells:

    1. The initialisation is the part of the original algorithm that scales the worst. The greedy column subset selection needs a full K^2 column for every candidate cell, which is O(N^2) and simply will not finish on millions of cells. bixverse therefore switches strategy by size: above greedy_threshold (20,000 cells by default) it drops the greedy top-up and samples the archetypes at random, which is effectively free. When a better-than-random start is wanted but the greedy pass is still out of reach, setting n_landmarks turns on a Nyström route: a small set of density-weighted landmarks is chosen (5 to 10 times n_sea_cells is a sensible range), the diffusion operator is built and eigendecomposed on those landmarks alone, and the multiscale embedding is carried to all cells via a Nyström extension before the usual max-min waypoint sampling. The eigendecomposition stays at landmark scale L x L instead of N x N.
    2. The optimisation loop itself runs in bounded memory. K^2 is never formed; every K^2 X term is evaluated as K (K X), so memory stays bounded by the number of non-zeros in K rather than N^2. Neither Frank-Wolfe gradient is ever materialised. The A update runs cell-major: a column of A is a convex combination of at most max_fw_iters one-hot atoms, so the solver carries (index, weight) pairs and patches the gradient with rank-1 corrections instead of rebuilding it from the sparse A on every iteration. The argmin over the two gradient terms is fused and runs on SIMD (NEON on Apple Silicon, SSE2, AVX-2 or AVX-512 picked at runtime on x86). The B update walks one gradient column per archetype in the same spirit. Everything is chunked across rayon threads.
    3. K^2 B is the one product the inner loop needs on every single iteration, so it is cached rather than recomputed. A Frank-Wolfe step changes B by a rank-k update, and the matching change to K^2 B is the same scaling plus one weighted column of K^2 per archetype; the pruning corrections fold into the same delta. The update is exact, and a full recompute still runs every eight iterations to bound floating point drift and the sparsity pattern. The B loop stops early once the relative Frank-Wolfe duality gap drops below 1e-3.
    4. pruning is on by default and should stay on. The Frank-Wolfe updates only ever add atoms, so without pruning the non-zeros in A and B climb monotonically across the whole fit and the time per iteration keeps rising instead of settling. The accuracy cost sits in pruning_threshold, not in the flag. Keep it below the smallest weight the schedule can produce, 2 / (T (T + 1)) for T = max_fw_iters; above that you start deleting live mass and shift the solution. The default 1e-7 removes numerical dust only.
    5. The RSS for the convergence check never materialises the N x N reconstruction K B A. The squared residual is expanded with the trace identity and evaluated through cyclic reordering, so every intermediate is at most N x k or k x k. Same Frobenius norm, just without the dense reconstruction.

    Most of that is automatic. The knobs you actually reach for on large data are greedy_threshold and n_landmarks for the initialisation, and pruning/pruning_threshold for the loop. Together they are what made it possible to run a million cells locally, which the original implementation cannot do.

    SuperCells¶

    SuperCells runs walktrap on the kNN graph. The number of meta cells is set indirectly through graining_factor: with a factor of 30 over ~6800 cells you should get roughly ~230 meta cells. The kernel-based version of SuperCells 2.0 from Hérault et al. is on by default. (The multi-modal versions are still to come. Watch the space...)

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    supercells = bv.metacells.generate_supercells(
    sc,
    params=SupercellParams(graining_factor=30),
    verbose=True,
)

    SuperCells on large data¶

    SuperCell is already far cheaper than SEACells on large data: there is no archetypal analysis, just Walktrap community detection on the kNN graph. The one part that does not scale naively is the random-walk representation. compute_walk_probabilities() within the Rust code gives every cell a sparse vector of landing probabilities for a walk_length-step walk; on a well-connected graph these vectors spread to touch a large fraction of cells after only a few steps, so the store drifts towards dense and memory grows as O(n x support).

    max_support caps this. With max_support = k each initial walk vector keeps only its k largest entries (the dropped tail holds negligible walk mass), bounding the store at roughly k x n regardless of how far the walks spread. This makes the run an approximation: the Ward merge criterion is driven by distances between walk vectors, and truncating them can shift the merge order slightly, so you may get marginally different communities than the exact run. With max_support=None (the default) the walks are kept exact. Beyond saving memory, a smaller k also speeds up every distance and merge operation, since both are linear in the support.

    supercells_large = bv.metacells.generate_supercells(
    sc,
    params=SupercellParams(
        graining_factor=30,
        max_support=256,  # would bound the walk vectors to 256
    ),
    verbose=True,
)

    MetaCells2¶

    MetaCells2 is the odd one out. It never touches the PCA or the kNN graph from above: it downsamples the raw counts per pile, picks its own feature genes, builds a balanced kNN graph on their correlations and partitions that with simulated annealing. Cells that look deviant within their candidate meta cell get pulled out and re-run, and whatever still does not fit is left unassigned. The size knobs are target_metacell_size (cells) and target_metacell_umis in Metacells2Params; the defaults (48 cells, 160k UMIs) are upstream's.

    metacells2 = bv.metacells.generate_metacells2(sc, verbose=True)

    MetaCells2 on large data¶

    The divide and conquer part is what makes this scale. Cells get split into piles of 8k to 24k cells (Metacells2DacParams), every pile is processed on its own, and the resulting meta cells are grouped into piles of similar meta cells for a second pass, so rare states that got spread across random piles end up together. Each pile holds two dense pile x pile matrices, so memory is bounded by the pile size, not the data size.

    Before any of that, rare gene modules are detected: genes expressed in at most 0.1% of the cells that co-occur. Their cells get piled separately, so a rare population of a few dozen cells does not get diluted across piles. On small data like this the step finds nothing, which is what upstream does too. Switch it off with rare_gene_modules=False.

    max_parallel_piles trades memory for speed. Each extra pile in flight costs another two dense matrices.

    from bixverse.params import Metacells2DacParams

metacells2_large = bv.metacells.generate_metacells2(
    sc,
    dac_params=Metacells2DacParams(max_parallel_piles=4),
    verbose=True,
)

    Metrics¶

    Purity¶

    A simple sanity check is to ask, for each meta cell, what fraction of its constituent cells share the same underlying label. We use the cell type labels that ship with the data as a proxy for cell type identity. The labels themselves are imperfect, so absolute numbers should be read with that caveat, but relative differences between methods are reasonably indicative.

    In [17]:
    Copied! 
    # memberships are positions in the full obs table, so the labels come from the
# unfiltered obs (here every cell is kept anyway)
cell_labels = sc.obs(cols=["celltype"])["celltype"].cast(pl.String).to_list()

meta_cells = {
    "hdWGCNA": hdwgcna,
    "SEACells": seacells,
    "SuperCells": supercells,
    "MetaCells2": metacells2,
}

for mc in meta_cells.values():
    bv.metacells.calc_meta_cell_purity(mc, cell_labels)

purity_df = pl.concat(
    [
        mc.obs(cols=["mc_purity"]).select(
            pl.lit(method).alias("method"), pl.col("mc_purity").alias("purity")
        )
        for method, mc in meta_cells.items()
    ]
)

purity_df.group_by("method", maintain_order=True).agg(
    mean=pl.col("purity").mean(), median=pl.col("purity").median()
)
    # memberships are positions in the full obs table, so the labels come from the # unfiltered obs (here every cell is kept anyway) cell_labels = sc.obs(cols=["celltype"])["celltype"].cast(pl.String).to_list() meta_cells = { "hdWGCNA": hdwgcna, "SEACells": seacells, "SuperCells": supercells, "MetaCells2": metacells2, } for mc in meta_cells.values(): bv.metacells.calc_meta_cell_purity(mc, cell_labels) purity_df = pl.concat( [ mc.obs(cols=["mc_purity"]).select( pl.lit(method).alias("method"), pl.col("mc_purity").alias("purity") ) for method, mc in meta_cells.items() ] ) purity_df.group_by("method", maintain_order=True).agg( mean=pl.col("purity").mean(), median=pl.col("purity").median() )

    def violin_by_method(
    df: pl.DataFrame, value: str, ylabel: str, ax: plt.Axes | None = None
) -> plt.Axes:
    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    methods = list(meta_cells)
    data = [df.filter(pl.col("method") == m)[value].to_numpy() for m in methods]
    parts = ax.violinplot(data, showextrema=False)
    for body, colour in zip(
        parts["bodies"],  # ty: ignore[invalid-argument-type] # matplotlib stubs type the violin parts as bare Collection
        bv.pl.bx_colors("main", n=len(methods)),
        strict=True,
    ):
        body.set_facecolor(colour)
        body.set_alpha(0.6)
    ax.boxplot(
        data,
        widths=0.05,
        flierprops={"markersize": 2},
        medianprops={"color": "black"},
    )
    ax.set_xticks(range(1, len(methods) + 1), methods)
    ax.set_xlabel("Method")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    return ax

    In terms of cell type purity, the methods are basically the same. Potentially more interesting is their behaviour in the manifold, see below...

    Manifold regions¶

    We called calc_diffusion_coordinates() with the kNN graph on the data. This tells us which parts of the manifold are being sampled here, e.g. high, medium or low density regions (based on the diffusion map and the distance to the 150th neighbour within that). This gives an idea how many rare cell states the meta cells capture.

    In [19]:
    Copied! 
    regions = ["high", "mid", "low"]
region_colours = {"high": "#2c2d54", "mid": "#969bc7", "low": "#6f9954"}

region_df = (
    pl.concat(
        [
            mc.obs(cols=["density_region"]).select(
                pl.lit(method).alias("method"),
                pl.col("density_region").alias("region"),

            for method, mc in meta_cells.items()
        ]
    )
    .group_by("method", "region")
    .len()
    .with_columns(proportion=pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum().over("method"))
)

    This is one of the most important differences between the methods. hdWGCNA disproportionally samples the medium density regions of the manifold and is basically proportion-based. SEACells on the other hand generates meta cells that capture sparse (more heterogeneous) regions of the manifold. SuperCells is closer to SEACells: few meta cells in the high density regions (13%) and a large low density share (42%, against 51% and 23%), with its mid share (45%) between the two. MetaCells2 looks a lot like hdWGCNA here, if anything with a stronger pull towards the dense regions.

    Compactness and separation¶

    We can also assess other metrics on the manifold representation. Compactness (how close are the cells within a given meta cell to the centroid) and separation (how far is the closest centroid). The first gives an (unbiased) indication of purity; the latter of diversity captured in the manifold. We can do this trivially via:

    In [21]:
    Copied! 
    for mc in meta_cells.values():
    bv.metacells.calc_manifold_metrics(mc)
    for mc in meta_cells.values(): bv.metacells.calc_manifold_metrics(mc)

    A long frame for the plots and the summaries:

    Some differences are visible here (lower compactness is better). Of the three kNN-based methods, hdWGCNA has the worst separation (not unexpected given the bootstrapping method only sampling direct neighbours, which also places most of them in the mid density regions). SEACells has the worst mean compactness (not surprising as the meta cells here capture more sparse regions of the manifold), and SuperCells (version 2.0, the default setting here) is both the most compact and on par with SEACells in separation. MetaCells2 comes out least compact, and the culprit is its low density meta cells (see the table below). Keep in mind that it is judged on someone else's turf here: the diffusion map sits on the PCA kNN graph, while MetaCells2 never saw it and built its own graph from the raw counts of the genes it selected per pile.

    def box_by_region(df: pl.DataFrame, value: str, ylabel: str) -> plt.Axes:
    _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    width = 0.25
    for j, region in enumerate(regions):
        data = [
            df.filter((pl.col("method") == m) & (pl.col("region") == region))[
                value
            ].to_numpy()
            for m in methods
        ]
        positions = np.arange(len(methods)) + (j - 1) * width
        # a method with no meta cells in a region gets no box
        keep = [i for i, d in enumerate(data) if d.size > 0]
        bp = ax.boxplot(
            [data[i] for i in keep],
            positions=positions[keep],
            widths=width * 0.9,
            patch_artist=True,
            flierprops={"markersize": 2},
            medianprops={"color": "black"},
        )
        for box in bp["boxes"]:
            box.set_facecolor(region_colours[region])
        ax.plot([], [], "s", color=region_colours[region], label=region)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(methods)), methods)
    ax.set_xlabel("Method")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    ax.legend(title="Density region", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc="upper left")
    return ax

    Based on this, we can conclude the following:

    • Purity is VERY similar across the methods (for this data set).
    • At matched K (~250 meta cells), SuperCells achieves the lowest median compactness, ahead of hdWGCNA and SEACells. Separation is comparable between SuperCells and SEACells, with hdWGCNA noticeably lower.
    • The methods differ markedly in where they place meta cells. SEACells assigns about half of its meta cells to low density regions versus under a quarter for hdWGCNA (and MetaCells2) and about 40% for SuperCells, consistent with its kernel archetypal formulation seeking out underrepresented states.
    • Method choice should reflect the downstream question. For tight aggregation in dense regions (e.g., bulk-like pseudo-replicates of common cell types), SuperCells is efficient and effective. For preserving rare populations or transitioning states (e.g., differentiation trajectories), SEACells' rare-state bias is desirable, with the trade-off of more heterogeneous meta cells in those regions. hdWGCNA is fast and simple but assignments overlap more in embedding space.

    Scoring external assignments¶

    calc_manifold_metrics() only scores meta cells that bixverse generated. If you have an assignment from somewhere else (SEACells in Python, a different parameter set, a clustering you want to compare against), you can score it in an existing diffusion map with calc_meta_cell_compactness() and calc_meta_cell_separation(). They take the diffusion map and one label per row; None marks cells that are not part of any meta cell. The rows of the diffusion map follow the kept cells of the parent object (sc.cells_to_keep order), so that is what the labels need to be aligned to.

    To keep it self-contained, we pretend the SEACells assignment came from an outside tool as a cell to meta cell table, and compare it against a random assignment with the same meta cell sizes.

    In [28]:
    Copied! 
    dcs = np.asarray(seacells.other_data["dcs"])
cell_ids = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "cell_id"])

# what an external tool would hand you: cell id -> meta cell
external = (
    seacells.obs(cols=["meta_cell_id", "original_cell_idx"])
    .explode("original_cell_idx")
    .join(cell_ids, left_on="original_cell_idx", right_on="cell_idx")
    .select("cell_id", "meta_cell_id")
)

assignment = (
    sc.obs(cols=["cell_id"], filtered=True)
    .join(external, on="cell_id", how="left", maintain_order="left")["meta_cell_id"]
    .to_list()
)

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
assigned = [i for i, x in enumerate(assignment) if x is not None]
random_assignment = list(assignment)
for i, j in zip(assigned, rng.permutation(assigned), strict=True):
    random_assignment[i] = assignment[j]


def score(assignment: list[str | None], name: str) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return (
        bv.metacells.calc_meta_cell_compactness(dcs, assignment)
        .join(bv.metacells.calc_meta_cell_separation(dcs, assignment), on="meta_cell")
        .with_columns(assignment=pl.lit(name))
    )


external_df = pl.concat(
    [score(assignment, "SEACells"), score(random_assignment, "random")]
)

external_df.group_by("assignment", maintain_order=True).agg(
    median_compactness=pl.col("compactness").median(),
    median_separation=pl.col("separation").median(),
)
    dcs = np.asarray(seacells.other_data["dcs"]) cell_ids = sc.obs(cols=["cell_idx", "cell_id"]) # what an external tool would hand you: cell id -> meta cell external = ( seacells.obs(cols=["meta_cell_id", "original_cell_idx"]) .explode("original_cell_idx") .join(cell_ids, left_on="original_cell_idx", right_on="cell_idx") .select("cell_id", "meta_cell_id") ) assignment = ( sc.obs(cols=["cell_id"], filtered=True) .join(external, on="cell_id", how="left", maintain_order="left")["meta_cell_id"] .to_list() ) rng = np.random.default_rng(42) assigned = [i for i, x in enumerate(assignment) if x is not None] random_assignment = list(assignment) for i, j in zip(assigned, rng.permutation(assigned), strict=True): random_assignment[i] = assignment[j] def score(assignment: list[str | None], name: str) -> pl.DataFrame: return ( bv.metacells.calc_meta_cell_compactness(dcs, assignment) .join(bv.metacells.calc_meta_cell_separation(dcs, assignment), on="meta_cell") .with_columns(assignment=pl.lit(name)) ) external_df = pl.concat( [score(assignment, "SEACells"), score(random_assignment, "random")] ) external_df.group_by("assignment", maintain_order=True).agg( median_compactness=pl.col("compactness").median(), median_separation=pl.col("separation").median(), )

    In [29]:
    Copied! 
    seacells_obs = seacells.obs(cols=["meta_cell_id", "compactness", "separation"])
check = external_df.filter(pl.col("assignment") == "SEACells").join(
    seacells_obs, left_on="meta_cell", right_on="meta_cell_id", suffix="_obs"
)

assert check.height == seacells_obs.height
assert np.allclose(check["compactness"], check["compactness_obs"])

    seacells_obs = seacells.obs(cols=["meta_cell_id", "compactness", "separation"]) check = external_df.filter(pl.col("assignment") == "SEACells").join( seacells_obs, left_on="meta_cell", right_on="meta_cell_id", suffix="_obs" ) assert check.height == seacells_obs.height assert np.allclose(check["compactness"], check["compactness_obs"]) assert np.allclose(check["separation"], check["separation_obs"])

    The random assignment is the floor: meta cells that are spread across the manifold have a large variance and their centroids all collapse towards the middle, so compactness goes up and separation goes down.

    Working with the MetaCells class¶

    This is where the in-memory representation pays off. HVG selection, PCA, neighbour graphs and embeddings on a few hundred meta cells take seconds and do not touch the Rust binary files on disk. We will just take forward SEACells here, but the methods below work across all of MetaCells.

    HVGs and PCA¶

    The same HVG and PCA functions you know from single cells work here...

    In [30]:
    Copied! 
    bv.pp.find_hvg(seacells, hvg_no=2000)

bv.pp.calculate_pca(seacells, no_pcs=30)
    bv.pp.find_hvg(seacells, hvg_no=2000) bv.pp.calculate_pca(seacells, no_pcs=30)

    Neighbours, clustering and UMAP¶

    The plot is much sparser than the equivalent UMAP on the original cells, which is the point: each dot is a denoised aggregate of ~27 cells on average (6881 cells over 250 SEACells), and the structure that survives aggregation is the structure that's robust to sparsity.

    Co-expression module detection on meta cells¶

    Meta cells compress information and reduce sparsity. That makes them ideal for co-expression module detection methods, and the SCENIC implementation within bixverse, akin to the single cell version, also runs on MetaCells.

    We need the human TF list from the Aerts lab (allTFs_hg38.txt from their cisTarget resources). The Python package does not ship a copy yet, so we fetch it from there. The genes in this data set are symbols already, so we only drop the TFs that are not in the data.

    In [33]:
    Copied! 
    tf_url = "https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/tf_lists/allTFs_hg38.txt"
with urllib.request.urlopen(tf_url) as f:
    tf_symbols = f.read().decode().split()

genes = set(seacells.var(cols=["gene_id"])["gene_id"].to_list())
tf_ids = [tf for tf in tf_symbols if tf in genes]

len(tf_ids)

    Consensus NMF on meta cells¶

    The same argument applies to matrix factorisation, and here compression buys you something concrete. Consensus NMF (Kotliar, et al.) fits n_runs NMFs, pools their components, drops the ones sitting on their own, clusters the survivors and takes the median of each cluster. What survives is the programme structure the restarts agree on. The catch on raw single cells is memory: every restart is dense, and they all live at once. On a few thousand meta cells rather than a few hundred thousand cells, n_runs=50 is unremarkable. This is the path where consensus NMF is genuinely affordable.

    Start by picking k. nmf_k_sweep() runs the consensus step across a range of ranks and reports stability against reconstruction error, keeping no factors.

    In [37]:
    Copied! 
    mc_k_sweep = bv.nmf.nmf_k_sweep(
    seacells,
    range(2, 13),
    n_runs=10,
    nmf_consensus_params=NmfConsensusParams(density_threshold=2.0),
)

with pl.Config(tbl_rows=11):
    print(mc_k_sweep)
    mc_k_sweep = bv.nmf.nmf_k_sweep( seacells, range(2, 13), n_runs=10, nmf_consensus_params=NmfConsensusParams(density_threshold=2.0), ) with pl.Config(tbl_rows=11): print(mc_k_sweep)

    The usual rule is to take the last k before stability falls away, while the error curve is still coming down. Here it does not fall away so much as bounce: past the trivially stable k = 2 to 4, stability dips and recovers, which says the meta cells support several plausible ranks rather than one obvious answer. It peaks again at 7 and 10. We will go with the smaller rank for this vignette, but in reality it might be worth exploring both.

)

    With 10 restarts, a cluster of 10 is roughly a programme every run found. A cluster above 10 (cluster 4 here) means a run contributed more than one component to it, and a thin one (cluster 2) is a programme only some initialisations saw.

    w (genes x k) and h (k x meta cells) come back in the same shape the single-run nmf() gives you, so the activations drop straight onto the UMAP:

    Pseudo-bulking¶

    Pseudo-bulks are conceptually adjacent but solve a different problem. Where meta cells are dense aggregates designed to feed into co-expression and archetype methods, pseudo-bulks are coarse summaries (one bulk per sample-by-cluster combination, say) used as input to bulk-style DGE tools such as limma-voom, edgeR or DESeq2 to get around pseudo-replication problems and p-value inflation in cell-based DGEs, see Zimmerman et al.

    get_pseudobulked takes a dict of cell IDs (or indices) and returns either a dense array or a sparse CSR matrix. With assay="raw" it sums raw counts (what bulk DGE tools expect); with assay="norm" it averages normalised counts.

    In [43]:
    Copied! 
    cl_df = sc.obs(cols=["leiden", "cell_id"], filtered=True)
cell_list = {
    str(k[0]): g["cell_id"].to_list()
    for k, g in cl_df.sort("leiden").group_by("leiden", maintain_order=True)
}

pb = bv.de.get_pseudobulked(sc, cell_list, return_format="sparse", assay="raw")

pb.counts.shape
    cl_df = sc.obs(cols=["leiden", "cell_id"], filtered=True) cell_list = { str(k[0]): g["cell_id"].to_list() for k, g in cl_df.sort("leiden").group_by("leiden", maintain_order=True) } pb = bv.de.get_pseudobulked(sc, cell_list, return_format="sparse", assay="raw") pb.counts.shape
    Processed group 10 out of 14 (took 2.91ms, completed 71.4%)
    Out[43]:
    (14, 12464)

    The returned matrix has one row per group and one column per gene. From here the standard bulk DGE pipeline applies: transpose it and hand it to bv.de.run_edger_ql(), in Rust, no edgeR needed. (The limma-voom twin is not ported to Python yet.)
